title: Programmable microbial consortia for durable ecosystem functions

concept.text: The innovation would be a reusable way to design microbial communities that carry out specified functions and keep doing so in the environments where they are needed. A consortium is a group of microorganisms working together; programming it would mean deliberately choosing its members and shaping their interactions, resource use and, where relevant, spatial organization so that their collective activity produces a desired result. The goal extends beyond finding a mixture that performs well in one laboratory assay.

Conceptual synthesis: durability means maintaining useful function despite relevant environmental variation, competition or invasion by other organisms, and evolutionary change. It does not necessarily require every member to remain at a fixed abundance. Functional performance, community composition and persistence of introduced organisms are distinct properties that would need to be measured separately. The proposed capability is reliable community engineering across several functions and settings, with explicit boundaries on where each design works.

significance.text: If achieved, this capability would make microbial communities practical engineering units: designers could specify a collective task, choose an appropriate community and predict whether its performance would persist under relevant conditions. This would be a substantial enabling advance in microbial ecology and biotechnology because community function depends on interactions among organisms and their surroundings, rather than simply on adding together the abilities of individual strains. The supplied BPA study provides a technical foothold through prospective community design and experimental degradation, while leaving the broader capability unachieved.

Bioremediation is the most directly grounded application. Reliable community design could help develop consortia for other contaminants and improve the consistency of treatment in complex microbial settings. The demonstrated BPA application supports this direction, but extending the approach to another pollutant would still require establishing the relevant organisms, interactions and environmental constraints.

Conditional synthesis: production systems could benefit from communities that divide metabolic tasks among members, while agriculture and medicine offer further possible applications. These outcomes require separate development and validation; success with contaminant degradation does not establish crop benefits, therapeutic efficacy or ecosystem restoration. The analogy to a programmable engineering component is therefore limited: living communities reproduce, evolve and interact with their surroundings, so a reusable framework would still need application-specific calibration and operating boundaries.

missing_breakthrough.text: The missing capability is a design framework that translates a desired function into a community whose performance remains predictable beyond its initial construction and assay conditions. The supplied study shows why composition alone is insufficient: collective interactions changed with toxicity, while native microbiomes can compete for resources or disrupt metabolic pathways. Environmental differences, including pH and nutrient availability, can also change whether an introduced consortium works. A framework must therefore connect community membership and interactions to function under changing conditions.

Proposed engineering barriers include determining which interactions must be measured, how much new experimentation is required when conditions change, and whether predictions remain useful in communities containing unfamiliar organisms. Spatial organization may affect access to resources and exchanges between members, but spatial design is a research dimension here, not an achievement established by the supplied study. Likewise, resistance to invasion and evolutionary maintenance of useful activity require direct investigation rather than inference from an initial improvement in degradation.

Proposed durability problem: designers must distinguish failure of the introduced organisms to persist from failure of the desired function to persist. A community could retain its members while losing useful activity, or its composition could change while the desired function continues. Resolving these possibilities requires measurements that connect functional output, population dynamics and evolutionary changes over an application-relevant duration. No such general capability is established by the supplied evidence.

current_state.text: In a Nature Microbiology article published on 29 June 2026, Mahmoud Yousef, Kiseok Keith Lee, Junivere Tang and colleagues reported interaction-informed models for designing synthetic microbial communities for bisphenol A (BPA) degradation. According to the supplied review of the main text and methods, the design library contained 16 bacterial isolate units: ten degraded BPA individually and six did not. Four isolate units were not strictly pure cultures. The earlier description of a design library consisting of ten BPA-degrading bacteria therefore omitted members used in the community-design experiments and overstated the purity of the starting units.

The researchers constructed community–function landscapes that related community composition and interactions to BPA degradation, then used those models to design new communities with predicted differences in performance. The reported dependence of collective interactions on toxicity is an important scientific distinction: an organism's contribution to community function need not be constant across environmental conditions, and individually non-degrading members were also part of the design library.

The soil application consisted of controlled laboratory slurry experiments using two soils containing native microbiomes, at two BPA concentrations, with uninoculated controls and technical duplicates. The authors reported increased BPA degradation following inoculation; in some conditions, the native microbiome did not degrade BPA on its own. This is a meaningful demonstration of a specified function in the presence of native microbial communities. It does not establish long-term persistence, resistance to invasion, evolutionary stability or deployment in an open ecosystem.

Evidence scope: the supplied review assessed the article's complete extracted main text and reported no extraction truncation. Figures and linked supplementary materials were not inspected, so plotted effect sizes and supplementary experimental details were not independently checked within that review. The available account supports the narrow experimental demonstration without supporting additional numerical claims about its magnitude or durability. The supplied record contains no bounded freshness-search results, so it cannot establish the field's latest status or whether another study had achieved the broader capability by 1 November 2026. That limitation does not invalidate the June 2026 result.

completion_criteria.text: Proposed demonstration: independent teams would use a common design framework to construct several compositionally defined consortia for distinct, preselected functions. They would specify functional performance thresholds, test durations and acceptable variability before evaluating the communities. These choices should reflect each intended use rather than impose an arbitrary species count or one universal duration. Starting compositions and any mixed isolate units would need to be characterized sufficiently for other teams to reproduce the designs.
completion_criteria.label: Independent teams use one framework for distinct consortium functions

completion_criteria.text: Proposed durability testing: each consortium would maintain its specified function against appropriate controls in relevant, varied environments over the prespecified duration. Tests would include deliberate challenges involving invading organisms and environmental variation, alongside measurements of community composition, persistence of introduced members and functional output. Evolutionary measurements would assess whether useful activity is retained through the tested period, and ecological measurements would assess effects beyond the intended output.
completion_criteria.label: Consortia maintain specified functions through environmental and invasion challenges

completion_criteria.text: Proposed reproducibility and practical boundaries: independent replication would test both the design procedure and the resulting performance, with failures and conditions requiring recalibration reported. Convincing evidence would show that the framework can prospectively guide new designs across the selected tasks, while documenting its experimental burden and operating limits. These are proposed evaluation criteria, not standards established by the supplied paper. Finite demonstrations would establish breadth across the tested functions and environments; they could not establish literal universality or success in every ecosystem.
completion_criteria.label: Independent replication tests design and performance, documenting failures and limits

related_concepts.text: Roster-based synthesis: MIC-02, “A predictive theory of microbial communities,” addresses the broader scientific problem of explaining and forecasting community behavior. MIC-10 focuses on using such knowledge to construct communities with durable specified functions. Better prediction could support design, but predicting a community does not itself demonstrate the ability to build a durable one. MIC-06, “A predictive whole-cell model for microbial design,” works primarily at the individual-cell level; it could inform member selection or modification without resolving interactions and persistence at the community level.

Roster-based synthesis: MIC-04, “Reliable nitrogen-fixing microbial partnerships for major cereal crops,” and MIC-07, “Programmable, reversible living therapies in the human microbiome,” are specific agricultural and therapeutic capabilities. Either could be achieved through a specialized approach without a general consortium-design framework. Conversely, MIC-10 would not by itself establish crop performance or the efficacy, safety and reversibility required for living therapies. These concepts overlap in the need to sustain useful microbial activity in complex biological settings while retaining distinct application requirements.

Roster-based synthesis: MIC-09, “Forecasting horizontal gene transfer and resistance spread in microbial communities,” concerns genetic change and dissemination within communities, which may affect the evolutionary durability and ecological consequences of a designed consortium. MIC-11, “Quantifying how environmental viruses control biogeochemical fluxes,” concerns viral influences on ecosystem processes, a potentially relevant source of variation for some consortium applications. MIC-12, “A causal map from microbial metabolites to host phenotypes,” could help define and evaluate host-related consortium functions, but causal mapping alone does not establish durable community engineering.

Roster-based synthesis: MIC-03, “Routine experimental access to microbial dark matter,” could expand the organisms available for community construction, while MIC-01, “An autonomously reproducing cell built from defined components,” addresses construction of an individual cell rather than a durable ecosystem function. MIC-05, “A general platform for targeted, adaptable phage treatment,” and MIC-08, “Broadly effective control of bacterial antibiotic persistence,” share concerns about controlling microbial behavior but target different capabilities. Access to more organisms, cell construction, phage treatment or persistence control would not individually establish MIC-10, and MIC-10 would not subsume those achievements.

change_log.change: Corrected the community-design library from ten BPA-degrading bacteria to 16 isolate units, comprising ten individual degraders and six non-degraders, and retained the qualification that four units were not strictly pure cultures.
change_log.reason: The supplied review identifies the main results and methods as more precise than the abstract's shorthand description.

change_log.change: Specified the soil demonstration as laboratory slurry assays involving two soils, native microbiomes, two BPA concentrations, uninoculated controls and technical duplicates.
change_log.reason: These details preserve the demonstrated scope and prevent the phrase soil remediation from implying open-ecosystem deployment.

change_log.change: Integrated interaction-dependent function, toxicity effects, competition from native microbiomes, pH and nutrient availability into the explanation of the design problem.
change_log.reason: These findings explain why a laboratory mixture does not establish a reusable capability for durable ecosystem functions.

change_log.change: Separated demonstrated BPA degradation from proposed spatial design, invasion resistance, long-term persistence and evolutionary durability.
change_log.reason: The latter dimensions belong to the innovation's research objective and were not established by the supplied study.

change_log.change: Expanded the proposed completion criteria to include prespecified thresholds and durations, disturbance challenges, independent replication, ecological effects and operating boundaries.
change_log.reason: These additions make durability and reuse assessable without presenting evaluative proposals as established standards.

change_log.change: Distinguished bioremediation's documented technical basis from conditional production, agricultural and medical applications, and clarified relationships across the supplied roster.
change_log.reason: This preserves the innovation's significance without treating downstream outcomes or neighboring capabilities as already achieved.

change_log.change: Preserved the review's figure and supplement limitations and the absence of a bounded freshness search.
change_log.reason: The evidence supports a specific June 2026 result but does not independently establish plotted effect sizes or the latest field-wide status.

unresolved_issues: Application-specific performance thresholds, test durations, invasion challenges and environmental ranges remain to be defined; the supplied paper does not establish a general completion standard.
The supplied evidence does not establish long-term functional persistence, evolutionary stability or ecological effects following open-ecosystem deployment.
The consequences of using four incompletely pure isolate units for precise compositional definition and independent reproduction remain unresolved in the supplied review.
Figures and linked supplements were not inspected in the supplied review, leaving plotted effect sizes and supplementary details outside its verification scope.
The empty bounded freshness-search record leaves the broader field's status as of 1 November 2026 unverified.
How much model rebuilding or additional experimentation would be required to transfer the approach across functions and environments remains unresolved.

brief.title: Microbe teams built for lasting useful work
possible: People cleaning polluted soil could choose a team of microbes—tiny organisms—that breaks down a chosen contaminant and keeps working as conditions change. A reusable design method would predict how the team's members work together and where their performance will last.
why: Reliable microbial teams could make pollution treatment more consistent. Designers could choose organisms for a shared task and predict their combined performance, which depends on their interactions with each other and their surroundings.

sources.who: Mahmoud Yousef, Kiseok Keith Lee, Junivere Tang and colleagues
sources.showed: Models linking community membership and interactions to performance guided bacterial teams that broke down bisphenol A, an industrial pollutant. Collective effects grew stronger as toxicity increased.
sources.quote: Designed communities are able to remediate BPA in contaminated soils.
sources.cited_for: Microbial interactions can guide the design of teams for pollutant breakdown.
sources.not_established: Laboratory soil tests did not establish lasting function under invasion, environmental change or evolution.

sources.who: Flor I Arias-Sánchez, Björn Vessman, Alice Haym, Géraldine Alberti and Sara Mitri
sources.showed: Repeatedly selecting and rearranging bacterial teams improved breakdown of an industrial pollutant. Some members helped the team despite performing poorly alone.
sources.quote: The best community after 18 such rounds of selection degraded the pollutant better than the best community in the first round.
sources.cited_for: Selecting whole communities can improve a chosen function.
sources.not_established: Improvement in a laboratory selection experiment does not establish durable performance across tasks and environments.

sources.who: Storme Z. de Scally and Michael J. McDonald
sources.showed: In a simple bacterial and yeast community, the bacterium protected the yeast from invading competitors. Longer shared evolution strengthened that protection.
sources.quote:
We find that the dominant spe-
cies (E. coli) in the community protects the less dominant species from being outcompeted during an invasion, and that this 
effect is strengthened by longer periods of coevolution.
sources.cited_for: Evolution together can strengthen a community's resistance to invading organisms.
sources.not_established: Protecting members of a simple community does not establish that a designed useful function persists.

sources.who: Chang-Yu Chang, Jean CC Vila, Alvaro Sanchez and collaborators
sources.showed: Computer simulations compared ways to select microbial communities. Earlier selection methods performed worse than simply screening communities after they had settled into stable populations.
sources.quote: We show that all of these protocols do worse than a simple screen, a no-selection control that has been largely missing from previous microbiome selection experiments.
sources.cited_for: Selection methods need comparisons against simpler ways of finding useful communities.
sources.not_established: Simulated community performance does not establish durable function in living communities outside the laboratory.

shown: Yousef and colleagues designed bacterial teams that increased pollutant breakdown in controlled laboratory mixtures of soil and liquid containing native microbes. This demonstrated useful activity alongside existing communities, but came from a single group.
missing: A common design method has yet to produce predictable teams for distinct tasks across independent laboratories.
Useful activity has yet to remain reliable through relevant environmental changes, invading organisms and changes over generations.
Independent replication has yet to establish the method's practical limits, including when designs fail or need adjustment.

milestones.label: Independent teams use a shared method for distinct tasks
milestones.explanation: Independent teams would use a common method to build communities with reproducible starting members for distinct tasks, with success criteria set beforehand. This would establish breadth beyond a single application.

milestones.label: Useful functions survive environmental changes and invading organisms
milestones.explanation: Teams would retain specified functions against controls through environmental and invasion challenges, while tracking members, evolutionary changes and wider ecological effects. This would test durability over the chosen period.

milestones.label: Independent replication establishes performance and practical limits
milestones.explanation: Independent teams would repeat the design process and test performance on new designs, reporting failures, needed adjustments and experimental effort. This would establish how reliably the method transfers within its tested limits.

uncertain: Appropriate performance thresholds, test durations and challenges depend on the intended use.
It remains unclear how much new experimentation is needed when the task or environment changes.
Some starting bacterial cultures contained mixtures; their effects on precise community design and reproducibility remain unresolved.

page.title: Predictive engineering of functionally stable microbial consortia
page.definition: A reusable design method specifies communities of microorganisms for different ecosystem functions and produces the predicted activity in their intended environments. Functional stability means retaining that activity through relevant environmental changes, competing microbes and evolution.

goal.need: In a metalworking-fluid study published on 7 September 2024, the experimental effort below produced a best community with a mean degradation score of 75.1%, measured by chemical oxygen demand relative to abiotic controls after four days. The authors described transferring the procedure to another problem as cumbersome. Separately, simulations showed that high initial function did not ensure retention of function after microbial invasion.

figures.caption: Experimental effort in the metalworking-fluid community-selection study.
figures.note: Culture measurements include repeated community compositions; these are not counts of independent selection experiments.

statements.body: Engineering Biology Research Consortium Microbiomes Roadmapping Working Group
statements.quote: functionally similar, but taxonomically diverse, collections of organisms in a microbiome, to maintain stable function across environments.
statements.context: The working group describes what its Functional Biodiversity roadmap theme seeks to engineer.

statements.quote: Optimize the functional robustness of engineered organisms in varying environmental conditions
statements.context: The robustness thrust of Biological Robustness in Complex Settings (BRICS); the programme confined its experiments to controlled laboratory settings.

completion.title: One design method produces consortia that retain distinct ecosystem functions in their intended environments.
completion.criterion: A published design method prospectively specifies consortia for distinct ecosystem functions. Each consortium meets functional endpoints throughout a duration and environmental, resident-microbiome and evolutionary challenges specified before testing in a published application protocol. Independent investigators reproduce the design-to-function result. This is an Atlas-proposed test; performance levels and durations come from the application protocols.
completion.set_by: Technology Atlas; proposed operational test for the combined capability.
completion.basis: Searches of EBRC microbiome roadmaps, DARPA BRICS, microbiome-engineering best-practice guidance, and standards and benchmark literature found no published completion test for one method combining prospective design, functional persistence and transfer between tasks. This proposed test combines those objectives without imposing a universal numerical cutoff.

milestones.title: A designed microbial community experimentally degrades a known compound.
milestones.criterion: A designed microbiome demonstrates partial degradation of a known compound; no minimum fraction is specified. Published on 29 June 2026, the bisphenol A study tested 10 designed communities in two soil slurries at 100 and 125 ppm, with two technical replicates per condition, and reported increased degradation following inoculation. This supports the laboratory criterion.
milestones.set_by: Engineering Biology Research Consortium, Microbiome Engineering, Distributed Metabolism, p. 58; this criterion concerns compound degradation.
milestones.threshold_quote: experimentally demonstrate partial degradation of the compound.

milestones.title: Engineered microbial guilds retain their function over time and after biological destabilization.
milestones.criterion: Functional guilds—microbes sharing an ecological task—retain their activity over time after destabilizers such as phages, plasmids or nutrient deprivation; no duration or tolerated loss is specified. Partial evidence: a 2025 E. coli–yeast community coevolved for 4,000 generations excluded 11 of 12 competitor strains in seven-day competitions, with five replicates per treatment and outcomes assigned by majority. That study measured coexistence and exclusion, not retention of an engineered ecosystem function.
milestones.set_by: Engineering Biology Research Consortium, Microbiome Engineering, Functional Biodiversity, pp. 46–47.
milestones.threshold_quote: Design guilds that maintain their function over time

milestones.title: A designed microbiome with multiple species per functional guild maintains function in a natural environment.
milestones.criterion: A microbiome containing multiple species per functional guild maintains its function in a natural environment. No uniform duration or permissible loss is specified. The bisphenol A soil-slurry experiment demonstrates contained activity alongside native microbes; it does not establish this natural-environment criterion. Achieving it for an individual community precedes establishing the reusable design method in the completion test.
milestones.set_by: Engineering Biology Research Consortium, Microbiome Engineering, Functional Biodiversity, p. 48.
milestones.threshold_quote: maintain their function in natural environments.

not_found: No cross-application standard specifying functional retention, challenge severity and test duration was found.
No independently replicated demonstration satisfying the combined completion test was found.

results.finding: Ten designed communities increased bisphenol A degradation in two soil slurries.
results.detail: The slurries contained 100 or 125 ppm BPA; each community was tested in two technical replicates per condition.
results.quote: Inoculation increased BPA degradation, and in some cases the native microbiome could not degrade BPA on its own (Soil 1, 100 ppm; Soil 2, 125 ppm).

results.finding: Ten designed communities increased bisphenol A degradation in soil slurries containing native microbes.
results.detail: The experiment demonstrated activity in contained soil slurries, not maintenance of function in a natural environment.
results.quote: Degradation dynamics depended on which community was inoculated, showing that composition affects BPA remediation even in the presence of a complex indigenous microbiome.

results.finding: Among 167 four-species combinations, the selected community degraded metalworking fluid by 75.1% on average.
results.detail: Degradation was estimated from chemical oxygen demand in laboratory cultures. The source identifies a commercial metalworking fluid mixture but does not establish degradation of a specific known compound.
results.quote: After 18 rounds of selection using a pool of 11 species isolated from MWF in which 167 combinations of four species were tested, we found a community that degraded 75.1% of the MWF on average.

results.finding: Of 11 species assessed after selection, Ct showed degradation of 51.7% versus 56.4% for its ancestor.
results.detail: The study compared evolved strains with ancestors after 18 selection rounds. Communities were repeatedly disassembled and reassembled, so this does not establish that an intact functional guild retained activity after a biological destabilizer.

results.finding: A designed gut microbial community in three bioreactors retained propionate production after acetate removal over a 460-hour experiment.
results.detail: The community contained functionally overlapping trophic guilds and was also exposed to an introduced species. After acetate was removed, propionate production was not significantly affected, while overnight acetate and butyrate concentrations declined. The three bioreactors were technical replicates.

results.finding: Eight-species Mix2, tested in six field replications, increased alfalfa biomass by up to 9.1% in the second growing season.
results.detail: Mix2 contained multiple nitrogen-fixing and IAA-producing species. Its field benefit declined over time and was not statistically significant in the third season. Nitrogen fixation was measured in the first season; persistence of individual inoculated strains in the field was not established.
